newsitem.title: TANZANIA: Rwandan refugees flee Tanzanian camp.
newsitem.headline: Rwandan refugees flee Tanzanian camp.

text.p: About 90,000 Rwandan Hutu refugees have fled a camp in northwestern Tanzania to avoid repatriation to Rwanda, a U.N. official said on Thursday.
Julie Johnson, spokeswoman for the U.N. World Food Programme (WFP) in Ngara, told Reuters the camp at Lumasi, which had a population of 113,000, was 80 percent empty.
"It appears the camp is virtually empty," Johnson added. "All commercial activity has stopped. The WFP warehouse at Lumasi camp was looted."
The flight from Lumasi brings to about 140,000 the number of refugees who have fled the Tanzanian camps, which originally held 542,000 refugees.
Earlier on Thursday U.N. refugee agency officials said some 35,000 refugees had abandoned camps at Kitale, Lukole and Keza and headed southeast in hope of reaching Zambia and Malawi.
About 15,000 refugees fled earlier in the week from camps in northwestern Tanzania. About 560 have crossed into Uganda.
An international aid worker who visited Kitale on Thursday said the refugees were leaving en masse and described the situation there as one of "complete confusion".

"Kitale camp is emptying out completely. Everybody is leaving. It is impossible to guess how many have left. I counted 40 people a minute leaving along a narrow dirt road. The whole camp is on the move," he said.

Officials blame the exodus on intimidation of the refugees by the Interahamwe, Rwandan Hutu militiamen who led the 1994 genocide in Rwanda. The Interahamwe are determined not to go home because they fear reprisals or prosecution.
Tanzania and the UNHCR had given the refugees until the end of the month to leave the camps and return to Rwanda.
Heavily armed Tanzanian army troops moved into the area around the camps on Thursday but it was unclear whether they would try to force the refugees back to their camps.
Another aid worker said security had broken down in camps abandoned by the fleeing refugees, most of whom were hostile towards the United Nations.
The Tanzanian army deployed heavily armed troops in Ngara after the refugees fled and the local radio warned the refugees they faced deportation or arrest for abandoning the camps.
It was unclear whether Tanzania, traditionally hospitable towards refugees, would use its troops. The army has some 10,000 men in the region but it has not yet tried to round up refugees.

The Tanzania-UNHCR repatriation plan has been attacked by the London-based human rights group Amnesty International and the exiled Hutu lobby group Rally for the Return of Refugees and Democracy in Rwanda.
The two institutions accuse UNHCR of abandoning its principle of protecting refugees against forced repatriation. Tanzania has not said what will happen to those who refuse to return voluntarily.
